titulo: Una restauradora de rotulos de neon
nota: Guion de produccion. El audio se genera con gen-listening.py; este fichero no lo lee la web.

lineas.texto: My name is Gemma Iriondo and I restore neon signs, which people assume is a job about lighting. It is mostly a job about glass.

I came to it from stained glass, and I was doing that for nine years before I ever bent a tube. The two trades share almost nothing except patience, and patience turns out to be the transferable part.

The commonest reason a sign fails is not the gas and it is not the glass. It is the transformer, and a transformer is the cheapest thing in the whole assembly. People telephone me convinced they need a new sign and half of them need a part that costs forty pounds.

The hardest colour to match is blue. Every workshop that made signs in the nineteen fifties mixed its own, and there is no chart anywhere. I match by eye against a photograph and I have been wrong often enough to be careful about it.

The job I am proudest of is a cinema sign in Bilbao. It had been dark since nineteen eighty-four and there were eleven letters missing. It took me four months, and the part that took longest was not the making. It was finding a photograph clear enough to work from.

What I refuse is fake ageing. Clients ask for it constantly. They want a sign that looks as though it has been there for sixty years, and I will not do it, because in twenty years somebody honest will have to work out which parts are real.

I have one apprentice and she came to me from dentistry, which sounds like a joke and is not. She had already spent years doing small precise work with her hands while somebody watched, and that is exactly the skill.

If you want to start, do not buy a torch. Buy a box of broken tube and break more of it. Everyone wants to make a letter in the first week, and the first thing you actually have to learn is how glass behaves when it is too hot, which you only learn by ruining it.
